narrative:
Your loan application was reviewed by an automated credit assessment system, which predicted a 58% probability that you represent a bad credit risk — a result that led to the denial of your application. While this is not an overwhelming probability, it was sufficient to tip the decision against approval. Understanding why this happened, and what could change it, is important for your next steps.

The system evaluated a range of financial and personal circumstances to arrive at this decision. To help explain the outcome, it is useful to think about "what if" scenarios — alternative versions of your situation where the prediction would flip from denied to approved. These counterfactual scenarios reveal which aspects of your profile matter most to the model's decision.

In your case, the analysis generated three such alternative scenarios, and the finding is remarkably consistent: in all three scenarios, only one single feature needed to change to flip the prediction — the status of your checking account. Currently, your checking account shows a negative balance (below 0 DM), which is the weakest possible standing in this category. Among applicants who were approved, only about 20% shared this negative balance status, while the majority had either no checking account or a positive balance. In all three counterfactual scenarios, the model determined that moving your checking account to a healthier standing — specifically to a status of "no checking account" or a positive balance — would be sufficient on its own to change the prediction to approved.

This is a striking result: not your loan duration of 42 months (more than double the approved applicants' average of 19 months), not your unemployment status (only about 5% of approved applicants were unemployed), not your installment rate of 4% of disposable income (above the approved average of 2.94%), and not your job classification — none of these factors needed to change in any of the three scenarios. The checking account status alone was the decisive tipping point.

That said, your broader profile does carry several compounding risk signals that likely contributed to pushing the probability toward the denial threshold in the first place. Your loan duration is unusually long, your employment situation is currently unstable, and your installment burden is relatively high. These factors together create a picture that the model finds concerning, even if the checking account status is the single lever that crosses the threshold.

The most actionable insight from this analysis is clear: resolving the negative balance in your checking account would be the most direct path toward a favorable reassessment. If you are able to bring your account out of overdraft — or if you hold a separate account with a stable or positive balance that could be referenced — this single change appears sufficient to shift the model's decision. It would also be worth considering whether reapplying after a period of employment, or with a shorter loan duration, could further strengthen your profile and reduce the underlying risk signals that made the checking account status so pivotal in the first place.
